newsitem.title: USA: Dow seen higher at open.
newsitem.headline: Dow seen higher at open.

text.p: A $13 billion merger deal between McDonnell Douglas Corp and Boeing Co is expected to help push Wall Street stocks higher at the open.

Both stocks were quoted sharply higher ahead of the open, with McDonnell Douglas traded at 64 on the Instinet system, up from a close of 52 on Friday, while Boeing trded at 105, up from its Friday close of 96-3/4.
In addition to the merger news, high tech stocks, which have taken a beaten recently, were set to open higher after posting overnight gains in London.

"We are going to open on a firm note," said Larry Wachtel, analyst at Prudential Securities. "Stocks are higher in Europe and the McDonnell Douglas-Boeing deal is certainly a blockbuster. That will help sentiment.

"It creates $13 billion of wealth and that is part of the supply and demand equation. We have done over $600 billion in deals this year, and whenever you do a deal you create buying new buying power."
He said that other defense suppliers like Lockheed Martin Corp and Raytheon Co could get a boost from the merger.
Boeing President and chief executive officer Phil Condit said he expected the merger with McDonnell Douglas to be accretive to earnings immediately.
The Dow Industrials rebounded on Friday, closing about a point higher at 6304 after losing 77 points for the week.
"Friday was a stabilizing day and should create at least a modicum of strength for today," he said.
In Tokyo, the Nikkei Average was up 80.65 points at 20,422.04.
In London, the FTSE 100 Index was up 19 points at 3991.
Among U.S. shares traded in London, McDonnell Douglas shares were up 13 at 65 while Boeing shares climbed 5-1/2 to 102-1/4. Coca-Cola shares added 1/4 to 48-1/8. Shares of PepsiCo shed 1/8 to 29.

Technology shares rebounded after Friday's broad decline. IBM was up 3/8 at 152-3/4, Intel Corp was up 1/2 at 132-7/8, Texas Instruments added 1/4 to 65-3/4 and Digital Equipment Corp rose 1/4 to 39-1/4.
U.S. Treasuries were thinly mixed, with the long bond unchanged to yield 6.58 percent.
The dollar was firm but off its highs in Europe and little changed in Tokyo.
The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street writes that market players are speculating about the motive for Microsoft Corp's convertible preferred-share issue.
